title: GOD CALLED HER “THE DELIGHT OF YOUR EYES”… THEN TOLD EZEKIEL SHE WAS GOING TO DIE.
paragraphs: GOD CALLED HER “THE DELIGHT OF YOUR EYES”… THEN TOLD EZEKIEL SHE WAS GOING TO DIE.
The heartbreaking night a prophet lost the woman he loved—and the terrifying truth about grief, judgment, and the God who would one day give His own Son to save us.
What do you do when the God you have spent your life serving tells you that tomorrow, the person you love most will be gone?
Not a stranger.
Not an enemy.
Not someone whose absence would barely disturb your routine.
Your wife.

The woman whose voice made an ordinary house feel like home. The woman who knew the tiredness behind your eyes when everyone else saw only a prophet. The woman who had watched you carry burdens other people could never understand.
And God didn't speak about her as though she were insignificant.
He called her something so tender that, thousands of years later, it can still make a grown man stop reading.
“The delight of your eyes.”
Then came the announcement.
She was going to be taken from him.
And what God told Ezekiel to do afterward may be even harder to understand than the announcement itself.
Because Ezekiel was not permitted to mourn publicly in the ordinary way.
Read that again.
A faithful prophet. A beloved wife. A death announced by God. And a command that seemed to leave no room for the grief tearing through his chest.

If you've ever buried someone you begged God to heal, watched a marriage collapse while you were praying for restoration, or stood in a hospital corridor wondering why heaven seemed silent, there is something in this account you need to hear.
But please don't rush to the comforting part.
Because Scripture doesn't rush there.
And if we turn Ezekiel's pain into a quick inspirational slogan, we may miss what God was actually saying.
In Ezekiel 24:15–18, the prophet records one of the most devastating moments in his ministry.
The word of the LORD came to him.
In verse 16, God said:
“Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke.” — Ezekiel 24:16, KJV
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ — maḥmad ʿênêkha
It means something precious, desirable, or delightful to your eyes.
The Hebrew expression is not merely describing physical beauty. In this context, it identifies someone deeply treasured by Ezekiel.
The woman was not named in the passage.
We are not told how they met, how many years they shared, whether they had children, or what their final private conversation sounded like.
We must not invent those details.
But God Himself acknowledged her preciousness to her husband.
And that matters.
Because the Bible does not present Ezekiel as a man incapable of affection.
It presents him as a man who loved someone deeply.
The next words are almost unbearable.
God instructed him not to perform the customary public acts of mourning.
He was to refrain from the usual lamentation and tears, keep his head covering in place, wear his sandals, and avoid the customary mourning practices described in the passage.
Then Ezekiel writes with a simplicity that makes the entire scene more painful.
“So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.” — Ezekiel 24:18, KJV
That is all he says.
In the morning, he spoke.
In the evening, his wife died.
The following morning, he obeyed.
No dramatic description of her final breath.
No account of his last words to her.
No explanation of what happened inside his heart when the house became quiet.
Just a single sentence containing a lifetime of loss.
And sometimes that is exactly what grief looks like.
The world expects a story.
But all you can manage is a sentence.
“She died last night.”
“He isn't coming home.”
“The doctors couldn't save her.”
“We lost the baby.”
“The marriage is over.”
And behind those few words is an entire world nobody else can see.
Perhaps you know that world.
You still remember the last conversation. The empty chair. The familiar belongings that suddenly became unbearable to touch.
You remember reaching for your phone before realizing there was nobody left to answer.
And somewhere inside the sorrow, a question begins to form.
Lord, if You knew how much I loved them, why did You allow this?
Ezekiel's account does not give us permission to pretend that question is small.
But it does require us to understand something crucial.
God was not establishing a universal command that faithful people must suppress their grief.
Ezekiel's response was a specific prophetic sign given at a specific moment in Israel's history.
Jerusalem was approaching catastrophe.
The people had repeatedly rejected God's warnings, practiced idolatry, and persisted in injustice. The judgment announced through the prophets was coming upon the city and its sanctuary.
In Ezekiel 24:21, God identifies the temple as the people's cherished possession, describing it as the pride of their strength and the desire of their eyes.
The same kind of language used for Ezekiel's beloved wife was now applied to something the nation treasured.
That connection was intentional.
Ezekiel's personal loss became a sign of the national devastation that was approaching.
The temple would be profaned. Jerusalem would fall. Families would experience losses they could scarcely comprehend.
And the people would be so overwhelmed by the disaster that the ordinary rituals of mourning would not unfold as expected.
When the people asked Ezekiel what his behavior meant, God supplied the explanation in Ezekiel 24:19–24.
His obedience was not a demonstration that tears are sinful.
It was a prophetic warning that judgment was real.
And here is where this account becomes deeply uncomfortable.
Something can be precious to us and still be unable to save us.
The temple was sacred, but the people had begun treating its presence as though it guaranteed their safety regardless of their rebellion.
They possessed a holy building while resisting the holy God whose name was associated with it.
They treasured the visible symbol while refusing the covenant faithfulness it demanded.
They wanted the reassurance of God's presence without surrendering to His authority.
And before we condemn them too quickly, perhaps we should examine our own hearts.
We can love the appearance of Christianity while resisting the Christ at its center.
We can post Bible verses and privately nourish bitterness.
We can sing about surrender while protecting the very sin God is calling us to confess.
We can attend worship, defend religious traditions, and speak passionately about faith while neglecting mercy, truth, repentance, and love.
We can become more concerned with looking spiritually alive than actually walking with Jesus.
The people of Jerusalem were about to discover that possessing something associated with God was not the same as living faithfully before Him.
And that warning has not expired.
But there is another danger here.
We must not twist Ezekiel's story into a weapon against suffering people.
If your husband died, that does not mean God was punishing you for loving him too much.
If your child became ill, that does not mean you made your child an idol.
If you lost someone precious, you must not automatically assume God was using their death to expose some secret sin.
Ezekiel 24 describes a particular prophetic judgment. It does not authorize us to diagnose the cause of another person's tragedy.
Jesus Himself rejected the assumption that every tragedy can be traced to the particular sins of its victims.
In Luke 13:1–5, He warned His listeners against treating those who suffered violent or accidental deaths as worse sinners than everyone else. Instead, He called all people to repentance.
And in John 9:1–3, when His disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus rejected their proposed explanation.
We must be careful not to claim knowledge God has not given us.
Some suffering comes because of human evil.
Some comes because we inhabit a fallen world.
Some suffering remains mysterious to us.
And sometimes the most faithful sentence we can speak beside a grieving person is not an explanation.
It is simply:
“I am here.”
There is a reason this matters so much.
Because a wounded believer does not always need another person telling them why God allowed the wound.
Sometimes they need someone willing to sit beside them while they bleed.
And the Bible gives us room for that kind of compassion.
Abraham mourned Sarah.
David lamented the deaths of people he loved.
Job tore his robe and fell to the ground in grief.
The Psalms are filled with tears, questions, and desperate cries.
And Jesus Christ Himself stood before the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
John 11:35 says:
“Jesus wept.”
Two words.
Yet they destroy the cruel idea that genuine faith requires emotional numbness.
Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
He knew death would not have the final word in that moment.
And still, He wept.
Think about that.
Knowing that resurrection is possible does not make grief meaningless.
Christian hope does not demand that we stop loving those we have lost.
It teaches us to grieve in the presence of a Savior who has entered human sorrow Himself.
That is why Ezekiel's silence must never be confused with the absence of pain.
Scripture tells us what he did.
It does not tell us that his heart was untouched.
And if you have ever had to keep functioning while your world was collapsing, perhaps you understand that distinction.
You can obey God while feeling shattered.
You can pray while struggling to find words.
You can trust His character while admitting you do not understand His ways.
You can believe in resurrection and still cry at a funeral.
Faith is not always a triumphant shout.
Sometimes it is a trembling voice whispering:
“Lord, I don't understand. But I am still here.”
And there is something else we must face.
Ezekiel's wife was not merely an illustration.
She was a real woman.
A real life ended.
A real husband endured the loss.
Her death became part of a prophetic sign, but that does not make her humanity disposable.
We should never celebrate her death as though the pain itself were beautiful.
Death is an enemy, not a romantic spiritual lesson.
First Corinthians 15:26 calls death “the last enemy.”
And that single description should change the way we speak about bereavement.
We do not need to call death good in order to believe God is good.
We do not need to pretend every loss feels meaningful in order to trust that God remains sovereign.
We do not need to explain away the horror of a grave to proclaim the hope of resurrection.
The Gospel gives us something stronger than denial.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story of Ezekiel opens toward something far greater than the sorrow of one prophet.
Centuries after Ezekiel's ministry, the Son of God entered the very world where beloved people die.
He did not remain distant from human anguish.
He took on flesh.
He experienced hunger, exhaustion, rejection, betrayal, and sorrow.
He loved real people.
He wept at a tomb.
And in Gethsemane, as the cross approached, He said:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.” — Matthew 26:38, KJV
In the Greek text, the word translated “exceeding sorrowful” is:
περίλυπος — perílypos
It conveys profound distress or overwhelming sorrow.
Jesus did not pretend that suffering was easy.
He did not approach the cross as though pain were imaginary.
He prayed.
He submitted to the Father's will.
And He went forward in obedience.
Not because suffering itself is holy.
But because His saving mission was holy.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God willingly gave His life for sinners.
Ezekiel's wife was taken from her husband as part of a unique prophetic sign.
Jesus, by contrast, willingly laid down His own life in accordance with the Father's saving purpose.
These are not identical events, and Scripture does not directly present Ezekiel's wife as a prophecy of Christ.
But when we read the whole Bible, we encounter the God who judges sin and the Savior who bears sin's penalty for His people.
The judgment Ezekiel announced was not an empty threat.
And the grace revealed in Jesus is not an empty promise.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we had cleaned up our lives.
Not when our private habits finally matched our public testimonies.
Not when we had earned the right to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And three days after His crucifixion, the tomb was empty.
Jesus rose bodily from the dead.
The resurrection does not erase every funeral Christians must attend in this present age.
But it changes what death can ultimately claim over those who belong to Christ.
In John 11:25, Jesus says:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
Notice what He does not say.
He does not merely say that He can explain resurrection.
He does not merely offer a religious philosophy for coping with loss.
He identifies Himself as the resurrection and the life.
Our hope is not rooted in our ability to remain emotionally strong.
Our hope is rooted in a living Savior.
And perhaps this is the part someone reading right now needs more than anything else.
You have been trying to make sense of something that still hurts.
You have been carrying questions you are almost afraid to pray aloud.
Maybe you are angry.
Maybe you feel abandoned.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that a stronger Christian would have recovered by now.
But listen carefully.
Your tears do not automatically mean your faith has failed.
The question is not whether you can manufacture a smile while your heart is breaking.
The question is whether you will bring your broken heart to Jesus instead of hiding it from Him.
He does not require you to pretend.
He calls you to come.
Matthew 11:28 records His invitation:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
Not only those with impressive testimonies.
Not only those who have already overcome their struggles.
Not only those who have mastered the language of spiritual confidence.
The weary.
The burdened.
The ones who know they need Him.
And if your grief has exposed something else—bitterness, unbelief, hidden sin, or a heart that has wandered far from God—do not run farther away.
Repentance is not an invitation to despair.
It is a call to turn toward the mercy available in Christ.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoéō, meaning to repent or change one's mind, with biblical repentance involving a genuine turning toward God.
Repentance is more than feeling guilty for a moment.
It is turning from sin and entrusting yourself to Jesus.
And forgiveness is not something we purchase with religious performance.
It is received through the grace of God in Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
This means you cannot buy God's acceptance.
You cannot earn forgiveness by donating money.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no financial contribution could ever accomplish.
He is the Savior.
Not our generosity.
Not our ministry involvement.
Not our religious reputation.
And that truth should make Christian generosity more beautiful, not less.
Because when grace transforms a heart, giving can become an expression of gratitude rather than a transaction driven by fear.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or forced, because God loves a cheerful giver.
For those who choose to participate, it can be part of their broader practice of Christian generosity—an additional ministry offering given freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.
And we want that invitation to come from the right place.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But from a shared desire to make the truth of Jesus Christ more accessible to people who desperately need to hear it.
Because somewhere, someone is reading words like these while fighting a battle nobody around them knows about.
A widow may be reading alone tonight.
A father may be trying to pray after burying his child.
A young believer may be questioning whether God still cares.
Someone who has been living in secret sin may be wondering whether forgiveness is still possible.
Someone may have stopped opening their Bible because every page reminds them of prayers that seemed unanswered.
And perhaps an article shared at the right moment could encourage that person to open Scripture again, seek help, return to Christian fellowship, or cry out to Christ.
We cannot promise what any particular article will accomplish.
Only God can change a human heart.
But we can faithfully keep pointing people toward the One who can.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior.
Not entertainment disguised as Christianity.
Not emotional manipulation dressed in religious language.
But the conviction that the Word of God deserves to be proclaimed with clarity, reverence, courage, and compassion.
And there is more available to help you grow.
These resources are meant to encourage biblical learning, spiritual maturity, prayer, and a closer walk with the Lord.
These items are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith-centered reading, reflection, conversation, and everyday reminders of biblical truth.
If you have been strengthened by this ministry, and you are financially able and prayerfully willing to help us continue and expand its work, we invite you to become a monthly supporter.
Not merely because you agree with it.
Someone may be silently wondering whether God is cruel because they misunderstood a difficult passage of Scripture.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus wept.
Someone may need to be reminded that repentance is still possible, that grace is still available, and that the resurrection of Christ is more than a comforting religious phrase.
And if one person comes to read God's Word more carefully because you shared this, that is reason enough to be grateful.
If a grieving person comes to mind, consider sending this privately with a gentle personal message rather than publicly drawing attention to their pain.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still exploring Christianity to follow along.
Not because following a page makes someone a disciple.
But because every opportunity to encounter biblical truth can become an invitation to seek the Lord more deeply.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a performance.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes a simple admission can become the beginning of an honest conversation.
Have you ever loved God while struggling to understand what He allowed?
Have you ever continued praying even when your heart was exhausted?
Have you ever found yourself standing between faith and grief, unwilling to abandon Jesus but unable to pretend everything was fine?
You do not have to explain the details.
You do not have to expose wounds that are still too tender to discuss publicly.
And if God has carried you through a season of devastating loss, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage another believer who cannot yet imagine surviving what they are facing.
Let the comments become a place for compassion, Scripture, prayer, and encouragement rather than judgment.
Because there are people who can quote Romans 8:28 and still go home to an empty bedroom.
There are people who believe in heaven and still miss the sound of a loved one's laughter.
There are people who know that Christ is risen and still tremble when another hospital calls.
And they do not need us to shame them for being human.
They need the truth spoken in love.
Now return with me to Ezekiel.
To that terrible evening.
To the sentence that Scripture refuses to soften.
“And at even my wife died.”
He had preached in the morning.
His wife died that evening.
And the next morning, he did what God commanded.
We are not told what the rest of his life felt like without her.
We are not told whether he ever stopped missing her.
We are not told the private conversations he may have had with God after that day.
The silence of Scripture should keep us humble.
But what we are told is enough to confront us with the seriousness of God's holiness, the reality of judgment, and the costliness of a prophet's calling.
And when we turn from Ezekiel to Jesus, we find the Savior who entered a world filled with such grief.
The One who wept.
The One who suffered.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One who will ultimately bring His people into a creation where death will be no more.
Revelation 21:4 declares that God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will pass away.
That promise does not mean your tears today are insignificant.
It means they are not the final chapter.
The Christian hope is not that every earthly story will end the way we wanted.
It is that Jesus Christ will bring His redeemed people into a future that death cannot destroy.
And this is why our theme matters so deeply.
Not because Jesus promises to reverse every tragedy before this life ends.
Not because following Him guarantees that those we love will never die.
Not because grace makes the consequences of sin, the pain of loss, or the wounds of this world imaginary.
But because the Gospel announces that sin and death will not have the ultimate victory over those who belong to Christ.
Your past does not have to be your master.
Your sin does not have to be your identity.
Your grief does not have to be carried without hope.
Through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, there is forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the promise of eternal life.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake admiration for discipleship.
Come to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His grace through faith.
And begin following Him, not because your life will suddenly become painless, but because He alone is worthy of your trust.
If you are already His, remain near His Word.
Remain connected to a faithful local church.
Seek prayer and support when the burden becomes heavy.
Keep growing.
Keep turning from sin.
Keep remembering the cross.
And keep looking toward the resurrection.
Because Ezekiel's account reminds us that even the most treasured things in this world can be taken from our sight.
But the Gospel reveals a Savior whose victory over death cannot be taken away.
The delight of Ezekiel's eyes was taken from him in a single evening. But in Jesus Christ, God has given His people a hope that even the grave cannot bury.
